analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal rulemaking to require agencies to pick the cheapest workable rule and defend costly ones in court-style hearings.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in May 2013, it received one subcommittee hearing in March 2014 and died when the 113th Congress ended with no committee or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change how federal agencies write major regulations. For any rule costing the economy $100 million or more, agencies would have to adopt the least costly option that meets the law's goals, justify in writing why benefits outweigh costs, and hold public hearings with cross-examination of witnesses for the biggest rules. Courts would review agency decisions under a stricter 'substantial evidence' standard. Supporters framed this as accountability and transparency; the practical effect is that major consumer, safety, and environmental rules become slower, more expensive, and easier to challenge — which falls hardest on the industries regulated, and secondarily on the people those rules protect.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries — energy, manufacturing, chemical, pharmaceutical, and financial companies facing costly federal rules — would gain the most. Every major rule would default to the cheapest option, could be picked apart at adversarial hearings, and would be easier to overturn in court. Well-funded companies are also the parties best equipped to hire lawyers and experts to exploit the new hearings and comment procedures.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing major federal rules

how_it_helps.text: For any 'major rule' (roughly $100 million or more in annual economic cost), an agency must adopt the least costly rule that meets the statutory objective, and may pick a costlier one only if it explains why the extra benefits justify the extra costs [S3][S2].

For the largest rules (roughly $1 billion or more), any interested party can petition for a public hearing with the ability to cross-examine witnesses on disputed factual questions, on the model of formal trials [S3][S2].
Courts reviewing major rules would use a 'substantial evidence' standard, and could no longer review the government's determination of whether a rule counts as 'major' [S3][S2].

The bill also adds genuine process improvements usable by anyone: electronic dockets, 60- and 90-day comment periods, public posting of the data an agency relied on, and a right for any person to petition for a rule's issuance, amendment, or repeal [S3][S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall on people who rely on federal safeguards — cleaner air and water, workplace safety, product and drug safety, financial consumer protections — because those rules would take longer to issue, would be written to the cheapest standard rather than the most protective one that passes a cost test, and would face easier legal challenges. Public-interest groups without litigation budgets would struggle to use the new hearing machinery that industry lawyers can.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: The least-costly-rule default would push agencies toward weaker versions of major safety, health, and environmental rules even in cases where the benefits of the stronger rule clearly exceed its costs, since the agency would have to justify departing from the cheapest option [S3][S2].

Adversarial hearings with cross-examination on scientific and technical disputes tend to favor parties with the resources to retain experts and lawyers, which is well-resourced industry rather than consumer or public-interest groups [S3].

Supporters' strongest objection to that critique: agencies now face little formal accountability for the cost of their rules, and the bill's dockets, cost-benefit analyses, extended comment periods, and petition rights would make rulemaking more transparent and open to ordinary participants, not just industry [S3][S2].

The bill would also slow rulemaking generally — proposed-rule notices expire after two years, and high-impact rulemakings would need extended comment periods and possible hearings — which delays protections even when they are eventually issued [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There are real merits here: more transparent dockets, longer comment periods, and clearer cost-benefit reasoning are improvements anyone can welcome. But the bill's defining features — a least-cost default for major rules, trial-style hearings for the biggest ones, and a stricter court standard — tilt the entire rulemaking system toward regulated industries, and the benefits of process transparency do not offset the likelihood of weaker and slower public protections. This is a structural change whose cumulative effect would be felt across every major rule for decades.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with bipartisan backing in May 2013, it sat in the Senate Homeland Security committee, got one subcommittee hearing in March 2014, and expired when the Congress ended with no committee vote and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Rob Portman (R-OH) introduced the bill on May 23, 2013 with eight original co-sponsors, including Democrats Mark Pryor and Bill Nelson, Independent Angus King, and Republicans Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Kelly Ayotte, Mike Johanns, and Joe Manchin [S3][S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, which took no further action on the bill itself [S5].
On March 11, 2014, a subcommittee on federal efficiency held a hearing on the subject; that was the bill's only activity beyond referral [S5].

It accumulated 13 cosponsors in total — 3 Democrats, 9 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but the full committee never reported it and the Senate never voted on it before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S4][S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: the rulemaking system as it existed stayed in place. Industries hoping for cheaper, slower, more challengeable regulation did not get it, and the existing web of federal health, safety, and environmental protections remained intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; existing protections stayed intact

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — Portman (R) joined by 9 Republicans, 3 Democrats, and 1 Independent — but no vote was ever taken, so that support was never tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (energy, manufacturing, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, finance)
industries.note: Had it passed, every major federal rule would default to the cheapest option and be easier to challenge, cutting these companies' compliance costs. The cost of that shift lands on the public in the form of weaker, slower health, safety, and environmental protections.

The bill creates new adversarial hearings, cross-examination rights, and judicial review openings that generate legal work; parties able to hire experts and lawyers benefit most, which favors large corporate litigants over public-interest groups.

The bill's transparency features — electronic dockets, published agency data, 60- and 90-day comment periods, and a right for any person to petition for new or repealed rules — are genuinely usable by small firms and citizens, not just large companies.
